title: Threatening with death
hook: if people don't fear death, why threaten them with it? (Tao Te Ching 74)

segments.voice: Yesterday, heaven's net: wide-meshed, and yet nothing slips through. Your line was heaven's net. Did you let one thing rest in it? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-six.

If you do that one more time, there will be consequences. It's a sentence that gets said in kitchens, offices and classrooms. Sometimes it works. Often it buys a few hours. And sometimes it gets the reply nobody wants: go ahead. At that point the threat is spent, and there's nothing left behind it. Chapter seventy-four of the Tao Te Ching takes that moment and pushes it as far as it goes, to the threat of death itself.
screen: `ONE MORE TIME, AND...` → `GO AHEAD.` → `A SPENT THREAT.`

segments.voice: First, the question. If the people don't fear death, the chapter asks, what's the use of threatening them with death? It's addressed to rulers, and it's a blunt piece of logic. A threat only works on someone who still has something to lose. Push people far enough and the biggest threat there is stops meaning anything. Second, the other side. Suppose people did always fear death, the chapter goes on, and someone did something monstrous, and could be seized and put to death. Who then would dare? It's not a call for more punishment. It's showing how thin the whole strategy is. Third, the carpenter. There is, the chapter says, an executioner who does the killing, an office that belongs to it. Killing in place of that executioner is like cutting wood in place of the master carpenter. And whoever cuts in place of the master carpenter rarely gets away without hurting their own hand. Readers differ on who the executioner is. Some say heaven, or the Tao itself; some say the proper course of things. Either way, the point lands: reaching for the ultimate power over another person wounds the one who reaches. Fourth, an ordinary Tuesday. The chapter speaks to rulers. But anyone can hold smaller blades. Do this or I'll leave. Do this or you're off the team. The chapter's question still works at that size: what happens when the threat stops scaring them, and what does wielding it do to your own hand?
screen: `A THREAT NEEDS FEAR.` · `HOW THIN THE STRATEGY IS.` · `CUTTING FOR THE MASTER CARPENTER.` · `THE SMALLER BLADES WE HOLD.` · then, large: `NO THREATS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one threat. Sit and let the breath slow down on its own. Then think of one if-you-don't-then line you've used lately, out loud or only in your head. With a child, a partner, a coworker, or with yourself. Hear it once more, quietly. Then notice the hand that holds it: the tightness in the jaw, the shoulders. Imagine setting it down. What could you say instead that asks, rather than warns? Let one sentence form. The bell holds the time.
Threatening with death. Chapter seventy-four: if people don't fear death, why threaten them with it? Whoever cuts in the master carpenter's place hurts their own hand. Today's word.
Your line: no threats. Today, when an if-you-don't rises, swap it for a plain request. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-four as a challenge to rule by fear: threats lose their force once people stop fearing them, and taking ultimate power into one's own hands harms the one who does it.

fork.setup: you rule, and the people no longer fear death. what does chapter seventy-four ask?
options: how can I make them fear it again?
what use is threatening them with death?
fork.reveal: the chapter asks what use the threat is at all, then warns that whoever cuts in the master carpenter's place hurts their own hand.

original.note: Chinese: the people do not fear death, the opening of chapter seventy-four.

trapdoor: what you thought: threatening with death is about ancient punishment.
what it means: a threat only works on someone who still fears it, and wielding it harms the one who wields it.
what a scholar hears: the 'master carpenter' line hangs on 斲, to hew wood; the executioner is read as heaven, the Tao, or the natural order.
